summary: The note is a long encyclopedic overview of senescence, or biological aging, covering its definition, variation among species, and the main theories explaining it. It describes evolutionary theories such as antagonistic pleiotropy, disposable soma, and mutation accumulation, alongside damage-based theories such as the free radical and DNA damage theories and the stem cell theory. It also covers biomarkers and aging clocks, genetic determinants, healthspan and its societal costs, and interventions including life extension and the anti-aging product industry.
one_line: An overview of biological aging (senescence), its variation across species, the main theories explaining it, and efforts to extend healthspan.
key_facts: Senescence, or biological aging, is the gradual deterioration of functional characteristics in living organisms.
The 1934 discovery that calorie restriction can extend lifespans by 50% in rats helped motivate research into delaying senescence.
Actuarial senescence is defined as an increase in mortality and/or a decrease in fecundity with age.
In 2013, a group of scientists defined nine hallmarks of aging; a decadal update added three more, totaling 12 proposed hallmarks.
A mouse is elderly at 3 years, a human is elderly at 80 years, and ginkgo trees show little effect of age even at 667 years.
Turritopsis dohrnii, the 'immortal jellyfish', can revert to its youth when it undergoes stress during adulthood.
More than 300 different theories have been posited to explain the nature and causes of aging.
George C. Williams proposed the antagonistic pleiotropy theory, in which genes beneficial early in life can be harmful later on.
Thomas Kirkwood proposed the disposable soma theory of aging in 1977.
Harman first proposed the free radical theory of aging in 1956.
Raymond Pearl described the Rate of Living Hypothesis in 1928, which links fast basal metabolic rate to short maximum life span.
Under normal aerobic conditions, approximately 4% of the oxygen metabolized by mitochondria is converted to superoxide ion.
Peter Medawar formalised the mutation accumulation theory of aging, stating that 'The force of natural selection weakens with increasing age'.
Mosaic loss of chromosome Y reportedly affects at least 40% of 70-year-old men to some degree, according to a 2022 study.
Over 2 billion persons are estimated to be age 60 or over by the year 2050.

entities.name: Planarian flatworms
entities.role: Have apparently limitless telomere regenerative capacity; not biologically immortal

entities.name: Ginkgo trees
entities.role: Show little effect of age even at 667 years

entities.name: Huntington's disease
entities.role: Neurological disease with onset on average at age 45, invariably fatal within 10–20 years

entities.name: Hutchinson–Gilford progeria syndrome
entities.role: Progeria disorder whose cause was reported in Nature in May 2003, showing DNA damage rather than oxidative stress is the cause

entities.name: Wilson's disease
entities.role: Hereditary copper-retaining defect whose symptoms resemble accelerated senescence

entities.name: Gompertz–Makeham law of mortality
entities.role: States that the age-dependent component of mortality rate increases exponentially with age

entities.name: Stem cell theory of aging
entities.role: Postulates aging results from stem cells failing to replenish tissues with functional differentiated cells

entities.name: Life extension
entities.role: Concept of extending human lifespan, modestly through medicine or dramatically beyond 125 years
